386: Discussion. Flavour integrates aroma, taste and mouthfeel and ranks among the strongest determinants of acceptance or rejection. It combines the volatile fraction with the sugars and amino acids liberated on cooking and with the texture of the grain, so that cultivars strong in aroma and moderate in firmness score well.
387: The same pattern has been reported previously. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) determined that flavour responds to processing more sensitively than instrumental measures do; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) that flavour improves with firmer texture until treatment becomes excessive; Roy et al. (2019) that flavour covaries with the bioactive and physicochemical properties; and Akter et al. (2025) that flavour and texture outweighed colour in overall liking. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Harinakhuri, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.

393: Discussion. Appearance governs the first impression and therefore determines whether the product is tried at all. It follows the colour coordinates, which are determined by pigment migration and browning, so that the cultivars remaining palest head the ranking.
394: Earlier reports corroborate this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that colour is among the two attributes most limiting to acceptance; Dutta and Mahanta (2014) that appearance constrains the market irrespective of nutritional merit; Srisang et al. (2021) that more severe processing yields a visibly darker product; and Akter et al. (2025) that a darker product was nonetheless more acceptable overall. The most favourable entry varied between products: Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Kataribhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.

400: Discussion. Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and the degree to which it corresponds to the requirements of the preparation. It is contingent upon the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and upon the protein network surrounding the granules.
401: Comparable results have been published elsewhere. Cheng et al. (2019) determined that heat and moisture yield a firmer, less adhesive network; Iqbal et al. (2021) that firmness follows the starch and protein network; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) that texture and colour jointly determine acceptance; and Devi and Badwaik (2022) that texture and pasting behaviour follow amylose content and starch structure. The leading cultivar varied with the product, Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Kataribhog ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

407: Discussion. Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. It is contingent upon gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose.
408: Comparable observations appear in the literature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) determined that cooking behaviour alters progressively with treatment severity; Kwofie and Ngadi (2017) that time and temperature constitute the processor's principal controls; Buggenhout et al. (2013) that cultivar and processing history operate jointly; and Cheng et al. (2019) that gelatinisation governs water uptake and cooking time. The leading position was shared between Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog and Harinakhuri, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
412: The analysis of variance addresses one attribute at a time, so that a single figure was required to establish which cultivar is superior overall. This was accomplished using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), in which each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) subsequently examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was placed on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 invariably denotes the superior outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights constitute a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 55, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 57.
415: On this index the superior cultivar was Gobindabhog for popped rice, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice. The control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, so that substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would improve the product without any alteration in the method of preparation. Table 56 gives, for each product, the cultivar exhibiting the best balance of attributes relative to the control.
420: The table below gives the five group scores and the composite score for every cultivar in every product, so that the standing of any entry may be read directly. The weights applied were sensory 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.
425: The weights above were assigned rather than computed, so the ranking was verified against a second set of weights derived from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was performed on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. This is the customary procedure for assigning weights to a composite indicator without recourse to judgement. The two rankings corresponded closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.952 and a minimum of 0.939, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 3 products, as Table 58 demonstrates. The ranking therefore proceeds from the data and not from the particular weights adopted. Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
428: The mean rank correlation was 0.952 and the minimum 0.939, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 3 products. The ranking is therefore not an artefact of the weights adopted. Where the two diverged, the cultivars concerned were in any case closely positioned on the index, so that the divergence is one of order between near-equals rather than of substance.
431: Cluster analysis was employed to examine how the cultivars and the products group together when all the attributes are considered simultaneously. The 30 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes determined in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them, the number of groups being set at 3. Where a cluster contains only one product, the method of preparation determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.
436: Of the 3 clusters, 2 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another to a greater extent than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) applied Ward's method comparably in rice and drew upon the cluster means to select genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to generate useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) advanced the same point from the product side, namely that different traditional preparations require genuinely different raw material.
439: Nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal were evaluated against Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar serving as the control, in the 3 processed products of this group. Each was grown and prepared identically for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. The principal finding is therefore unambiguous: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production is of markedly less consequence. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally retain its position in the next.
